title: Cascading Fallback Wargame and SLO Ownership Sync
summary: Tabletop wargame simulating cascading failures during a Private Deploy launch. Decided ownership boundaries for SLO/alert triage, updated runbook actions, and agreed on a short pilot to validate fallback policies. Several follow-ups: runbook edits, canary config, and a simulated incident drill next week.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-09-14 10:00 PDT | Duration 1h15 | Recording on | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Sofia (Product), Aisha (VP Eng), Liam (SRE), Nora (Reliability), Ravi (Runtime), Jordan (Infra), Ethan (QA)
--
[00:00] Sofia: Ok, let's get started. Thanks everyone for blocking. The goal for today is a tabletop, cascading fallback scenarios — we're focusing on Private deploy launch readiness and SLO ownership. We'll run through a couple of sequences, call out responsibilities, and capture any missing tooling or docs.
[00:15] Aisha: Quick ask — try to be concrete on owners and timers. We don't want fuzzy calls in a real incident.
[00:28] Liam: Agreed. I'll also surface what we already have in paging config; there may be overlaps.
[00:42] Sofia: Cool. First scenario: tiered capacity exhaustion in us-west-2 — primary runtime pool hits OOM for long-context requests, fallback to smaller quantized model variants causes CPU spike and then KV cache bloat, then the routing layer starts failing requests to downstream clients.
[01:05] Ravi: So layering: primary full-s-32 model -> fallback to s8-quant -> then fallback to s4-opt after CPU thresh. We haven't fully tested s8->s4 transition under load with prefix cache invalidation. The KV cache eviction pattern could amplify latencies.
[01:25] Nora: Important: when we do fallback we also need to reduce batching window, otherwise we get head-of-line latencies. But reducing batching reduces throughput and that's scary for customers.
[01:40] Ethan: QA note — our harness doesn't simulate continuous prefix/KV churn. I can extend it to evict and rehydrate KV entries rapidly, but need the acceptance criteria — e.g., latency p95 stays under X during fallback.
[01:58] Jordan: Infra question — do we have circuit breakers between routing and runtime? We have a per-route token bucket but not a global circuit that isolates a misbehaving model pool. That means a noisy fallback could take down other tenants.
[02:15] Aisha: That's risky. For Private deploys customers expect tenant isolation. Let's call this out as a gating item.
[02:28] Sofia: Ok, ownership call: who owns the SLOs here? At least two SLOs are in play: request latency SLO for interactive endpoints, and availability SLO for the Dedicated/Private customer. We need someone to be first responder for each during an event.
[02:45] Liam: SRE should be first-responder for infra-level degradation (circuit breakers, pool exhaustion). Runtime team responds to model-level degradation (quantization drop, OOM). But there needs to be a single incident commander. Recommend product on-call (maybe rotating PM) or a senior eng. Thoughts?
[03:06] Aisha: Product as incident commander for customer-impacting events makes sense for launch, but long-term we should default to engineering. For the pilot period, Sofia can act as IC for launch windows.
[03:22] Sofia: I can be IC for the first two weeks of the private deploy pilot. I'll coordinate with oncall SRE.
[03:32] Nora: On escalation: page SRE on paged severity 1, then runtime. Also include a fallback policy owner — who decides to change fallback thresholds live? That needs to be an engineering owner.
[03:48] Ravi: Runtime leads should own adjusting fallback thresholds, but only with an approved runbook step and logged change. We should not do ad-hoc thresholds.
[04:00] Ethan: We saw once when thresholds were changed ad-hoc the KV cache warmed and it flipped the other way, so let's capture that in the runbook.
[04:12] Sofia: Good. Next scenario: control plane partition — the control plane loses reachability to a subset of private deploy customers; routing decides to route to alternate region causing increased cross-region egress and latency.
[04:30] Jordan: If the control plane can't reach a customer's deployment, the policy currently is to route to hosted fallback unless customer opted out. We need to validate customer opt-out semantics for private.
[04:45] Aisha: Compliance note — some customers will have strict no-eavesdrop or no-egress policies; we must honor those by default and fail safeto 5xx rather than route to hosted. Put that as a mandatory pre-launch checkbox.
[05:02] Nora: Also, telemetry must capture the decision path — why we failed over: control plane timeout vs capacity. Otherwise post-incident it's hard to debug.
[05:15] Sofia: Action: add telemetry tag for fallback_reason and fallback_path. Who owns that?
[05:23] Ravi: Runtime + routing. I'll add a short PR to include tags in the router logs.
[05:30] Liam: We should also have a pre-signed audit log for private customers so they can see fallback events. That's on the compliance checklist.
[05:45] Sofia: Ok noted. Let's move to play-by-play simulated drill. I'll narrate: at T+0 the primary pool hits sustained 95% GPU mem and starts OOM killing; at T+2m routing flips to s8-quant, latency rises, p99 spikes. At T+6m KV cache eviction begins, error rates climb. At T+10m a neighbor tenant starts degrading.
[06:15] Ethan: Simulating that now in the QA harness — I see p99 jump to 2.3s when quantized fallback kicks in. Understood. The harness shows a pattern where if we don't throttle retries, the retry storms amplify.
[06:34] Nora: That implies we need per-client backpressure — maybe a rejection policy (503) with exponential backoff header instead of queueing.
[06:46] Jordan: We can add a Retry-After header and recommend client-side backoff in SDKs. But many customers use the raw HTTP API; we should still provide best-practice defaults in SDK.
[07:00] Aisha: Who owns SDK changes? Developer experience team but runtime must expose proper status codes.
[07:10] Sofia: We'll log that as an item. Next, decision tree on rollback vs degrade. If fallback increases latency but preserves correctness, do we degrade or rollback?
[07:26] Ravi: Degrade first if correctness preserved. Rollback is for correctness or data-corrupting regressions. Rollback has bigger blast radius and more customer coordination.
[07:38] Liam: On rollback, we need a warm standby plan. For model rollback we might need KV cache warmup— otherwise rollback could make latencies worse temporarily. So plan for cache pre-warm or cache rehydration script.
[07:55] Ethan: QA can script a warmup sequence to prime KV for the standby model. We'll need a way to trigger that automatically when rolling back.
[08:10] Sofia: Good. Let's capture the gap: automated pre-warm for standby models during rollback.
[08:20] Nora: Also, SLO ownership: define primary SLO owners (SLO owner, SLO responder). I propose a mapping doc: latency SLO -> Runtime team owner, availability SLO -> SRE owner, customer-notice SLO -> Product owner.
[08:36] Aisha: That mapping is fine as long as we also define the IC escalation path. Put it in the oncall rota doc.
[08:45] Sofia: I'll update oncall rota and include runbook link. Link to doc: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/cascading-fallback (note: placeholder)
[08:59] Liam: On alarms — we should tune the thresholds for p95 vs p99 and avoid double paging. Use a composite alert that only fires when both latency and error rate increase. That reduces false positives.
[09:18] Jordan: Composite alerts are available in the monitoring stack; we just need to publish the recommended templates.
[09:28] Sofia: Who will own publishing those templates?
[09:31] Liam: SRE will publish templates and share with runtime.
[09:35] Sofia: Great. Onto compliance gating. Security wants audit logs and KMS for private deploys. Any tech blockers?
[09:45] Jordan: We can integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping, but that adds latency on cold starts. Need to account for that in the SLO. Also HSM-backed KMS increases key retrieval times.
[09:58] Aisha: We must document the latency impact and get sign-off from security. Not a blocker but a tradeoff customers must opt into.
[10:10] Sofia: Next piece: exercises. We will run a live incident drill next week simulating the scenario. Liam, you schedule it. Nora and Ethan will define the witness criteria.
[10:22] Liam: Will do. I'll target 2026-09-22 and invite the oncall rotation.
[10:30] Sofia: Anything else?
[10:35] Ravi: One minor point — we should ensure the model catalog has explicit compatibility tags so routing knows which fallback is allowed per customer (some customers don't want quantized fallbacks because of hallucination risk). We need to tie that into policy.
[10:50] Nora: Add that to the runbook. We also need a customer-visible incident summary template for private customers. Product to own that template.
[11:00] Sofia: Ok, final recap — owners: Nora runbook edits, Ravi canary PR, Liam schedule drill, Ethan QA harness, Sofia update launch checklist. We'll meet for a pre-drill sync on 2026-09-21 to confirm readiness.
[11:20] Aisha: Also capture the blocker list: telemetry tags, SDK retry headers, pre-warm script. Those need to be in the launch gating doc.
[11:33] Sofia: I'll add them. Thanks everyone. We'll close and track action items in the runbook PR.
[11:45] (crosstalk) Jordan: Quick note — putting the circuit breaker in the routing layer should be prioritized top-3 for the sprint.
[11:55] Sofia: Noted. End meeting.
--
Post-meeting notes: rough transcription with some misrecognized tokens (KV vs K V, quant vs q8 sometimes), references to internal links provided as placeholders. Transcript includes natural hesitation and overlapping segments.
